choices.text: An initiator adds to the C=C bond of a vinyl monomer, and the reactive intermediate adds monomer after monomer
Two difunctional reactants form each bond of the chain stepwise, independently of the other bonds
choices.why: That describes step-growth polymers such as nylons and polyesters. Chain-growth polymers grow by a chain reaction through a reactive intermediate.

choices.text: Small molecules such as water are lost each time two monomers join
choices.why: Chain-growth polymerization adds the initiator and then monomer units to C=C bonds. Nothing is lost as each vinyl monomer joins the chain.

choices.text: Two alkenes exchange the substituents on their double bonds
choices.why: That is olefin metathesis, a different method. In chain-growth polymerization an initiator adds to the C=C bond and starts a chain reaction.

explanation: Chain-growth polymers are made by chain-reaction polymerization: an initiator adds to the C=C bond of a vinyl monomer to give a reactive intermediate, which reacts with a second monomer to give a new intermediate, which reacts with a third, and so on. The initiator can be a radical, an acid, or a base.

prompt: Why was radical polymerization historically the most common way to make chain-growth polymers?

choices.text: It can be carried out with practically any vinyl monomer
It works only with monomers that carry an electron-donating group
choices.why: That restriction belongs to acid-catalyzed (cationic) polymerization. Radical polymerization has no such limit, which is why it was the most common.

choices.text: It works only with monomers that carry an electron-withdrawing group
choices.why: That restriction belongs to basic (anionic) polymerization. Radical polymerization works with practically any vinyl monomer.

choices.text: It gives perfectly linear chains with no branching
choices.why: Radical polymerization of ethylene gives branched low-density polyethylene. The section credits radical methods for their broad scope, not for linear chains.

explanation: The initiator can be a radical, an acid, or a base. Radical polymerization was historically the most common method because it can be carried out with practically any vinyl monomer, while cationic and anionic polymerization each need a particular kind of substituent.

prompt: When benzoyl peroxide is heated to start the radical polymerization of ethylene, which radical adds to the first ethylene molecule?

choices.text: The phenyl radical
The benzoyloxy radical
choices.why: Heating benzoyl peroxide first gives the benzoyloxy radical, but that radical goes on to form the phenyl radical, which is the one that adds to ethylene.

choices.text: A hydrogen atom
choices.why: No hydrogen atom is involved. Benzoyl peroxide gives a benzoyloxy radical, which forms a phenyl radical that adds to ethylene.

choices.text: A carbocation formed by protonation of ethylene
choices.why: A carbocation would be cationic polymerization. Benzoyl peroxide is a radical initiator, and the phenyl radical adds to ethylene.

explanation: Benzoyl peroxide reacts on heating to form the benzoyloxy radical, which reacts to form the phenyl radical. The phenyl radical adds to ethylene to give a new carbon radical, and continued addition of ethylene builds the polymer chain.

prompt: Acid-catalyzed (cationic) polymerization works only with which kind of vinyl monomer?

choices.text: One with an electron-donating group that can stabilize the chain-carrying carbocation
One with an electron-withdrawing group that can stabilize the chain-carrying anion
choices.why: That is the requirement for basic (anionic) polymerization, not cationic polymerization.

choices.text: Practically any vinyl monomer
choices.why: That describes radical polymerization. Cationic polymerization is effective only when an electron-donating group stabilizes the carbocation.

choices.text: One with an electron-withdrawing group that can stabilize the chain-carrying carbocation
choices.why: An electron-withdrawing group would destabilize a carbocation. The section requires an electron-donating group (EDG).

explanation: In cationic polymerization the chain is carried by a carbocation, so the method is effective only with vinyl monomers that contain an electron-donating group (EDG) capable of stabilizing that carbocation intermediate. Isobutylene, (CH3)2C=CH2, is a good example.

prompt: Isobutylene (2-methylpropene) is polymerized commercially under cationic conditions. At what temperature is the reaction carried out, in °C?
explanation: The cationic polymerization of isobutylene is carried out commercially at −80 °C, using BF3 and a small amount of water to generate the BF3OH− H+ catalyst. Isobutylene polymerizes rapidly under these conditions.

prompt: What catalyst is used for the commercial polymerization of isobutylene, and what is the product used for?

choices.text: BF3 with a small amount of water; truck and bicycle inner tubes
Butyllithium; foam coffee cups
choices.why: Butyllithium is the anionic initiator used to make polystyrene for foam cups. Isobutylene polymerizes under cationic (acid) conditions.

choices.text: Benzoyl peroxide; plastic squeeze bottles
choices.why: Benzoyl peroxide is a radical initiator. Isobutylene is polymerized cationically with BF3 and a little water.

choices.text: Triethylaluminum with TiCl4; underground pipes
choices.why: That is a Ziegler–Natta catalyst, used for polyethylene and polypropylene. Isobutylene is polymerized cationically with BF3 and water.

explanation: Isobutylene polymerizes rapidly under cationic conditions. Commercially the reaction uses BF3 and a small amount of water to generate BF3OH− H+ catalyst at −80 °C, and the polyisobutylene is used in truck and bicycle inner tubes.

prompt: Which is the repeating unit of polyisobutylene, the polymer of (CH3)2C=CH2?

choices.text: –CH2–CH(CH3)–
choices.why: That is the repeating unit of polypropylene, from H2C=CHCH3. Isobutylene has two methyl groups on one carbon.

choices.text: –CH(CH3)–CH(CH3)–
choices.why: That unit would come from 2-butene, CH3CH=CHCH3, with one methyl on each carbon. In isobutylene both methyls are on the same carbon.

choices.text: –CH2–C(CH3)=CH–CH2–
choices.why: That is a unit from isoprene, a diene. Isobutylene has only one double bond, so its unit keeps no C=C.

explanation: Each isobutylene molecule, (CH3)2C=CH2, adds to the growing chain through its double bond, so the polymer is a chain of –CH2–C(CH3)2– units. The two methyl groups stay together on one backbone carbon.

prompt: In basic (anionic) polymerization of a vinyl monomer that carries an electron-withdrawing group, what is the chain-carrying step?

choices.text: Conjugate nucleophilic addition of an anion to the unsaturated monomer
Addition of a carbocation to the double bond of the monomer
choices.why: Carbocations carry the chain in cationic polymerization, which needs electron-donating groups. In anionic polymerization the chain carrier is an anion.

choices.text: Addition of a radical to the double bond of the monomer
choices.why: Radicals carry the chain in radical polymerization. The anionic method uses conjugate addition of an anion.

choices.text: Insertion of the monomer into a carbon–titanium bond
choices.why: That is the Ziegler–Natta mechanism (Section 31.2). Anionic polymerization proceeds by conjugate nucleophilic addition.

explanation: Vinyl monomers with electron-withdrawing groups (EWG) can be polymerized by basic (anionic) catalysts. The chain-carrying step is a conjugate nucleophilic addition of an anion to the unsaturated monomer (Section 19.13), giving a new anion that adds to the next monomer.

prompt: Which set of monomers does the section list as able to be polymerized anionically?

choices.text: Acrylonitrile, methyl methacrylate, and styrene
Isobutylene, acrylonitrile, and styrene
choices.why: Isobutylene has electron-donating methyl groups and is the section's example of a monomer that polymerizes cationically.

choices.text: Ethylene, propylene, and isobutylene
choices.why: None of these has an electron-withdrawing group, which anionic polymerization needs.

choices.text: Isobutylene, methyl methacrylate, and styrene
choices.why: Isobutylene is the section's example for cationic polymerization, not anionic.

explanation: Acrylonitrile (H2C=CHCN), methyl methacrylate [H2C=C(CH3)CO2CH3], and styrene (H2C=CHC6H5) can all be polymerized anionically. The polystyrene in foam coffee cups, for example, is made by anionic polymerization of styrene with butyllithium as catalyst.

prompt: The polystyrene used in foam coffee cups is made by anionic polymerization of styrene. What catalyst is used?

choices.text: Butyllithium
BF3 with a small amount of water
choices.why: That is the acid catalyst for cationic polymerization of isobutylene.

choices.text: Benzoyl peroxide
choices.why: Benzoyl peroxide is a radical initiator, not an anionic one.

choices.text: Titanium tetrachloride with triethylaluminum
choices.why: That combination makes a Ziegler–Natta catalyst (Section 31.2). Foam-cup polystyrene is made with butyllithium.

explanation: The polystyrene in foam coffee cups is prepared by anionic polymerization of styrene using butyllithium as catalyst. The butyl anion adds to styrene to give an anionic intermediate, which adds to more styrene, again and again.

prompt: Super glue is a solution of pure methyl α-cyanoacrylate, H2C=C(CN)CO2CH3. How many electron-withdrawing groups does this monomer have that make anionic addition particularly easy?
explanation: Methyl α-cyanoacrylate has two electron-withdrawing groups on the same carbon: the cyano group (–CN) and the ester group (–CO2CH3). Together they make anionic addition particularly easy, which is why super glue sets so readily.

prompt: What starts the polymerization of super glue when it is spread on an object?

choices.text: Trace amounts of water or bases on the surface
Heat from the surrounding air, which splits the monomer into radicals
choices.why: No radical initiator or heating is needed. The monomer polymerizes anionically, started by traces of water or bases.

choices.text: Acid on the surface, which protonates the double bond
choices.why: Super glue polymerizes anionically, not cationically. Its two electron-withdrawing groups favor anion addition.

choices.text: Oxygen from the air, which adds to the double bond
choices.why: The section names trace water or bases as the initiators, and skin is a good source of these basic initiators.

explanation: Methyl α-cyanoacrylate polymerizes anionically. Trace amounts of water or bases on the surface of an object are enough to start polymerization and bind articles together. Skin is a good source of basic initiators, which is why fingers get stuck together, and related cyanoacrylate esters such as Dermabond are used in place of sutures to close wounds.

prompt: Which order correctly ranks these monomers from least to most reactive toward cationic polymerization: H2C=CHCH3, H2C=CHCl, H2C=CH–C6H5, H2C=CHCO2CH3?

choices.text: H2C=CHCO2CH3 < H2C=CHCl < H2C=CHCH3 < H2C=CH–C6H5
H2C=CH–C6H5 < H2C=CHCH3 < H2C=CHCl < H2C=CHCO2CH3
choices.why: This is the reverse order. Cationic polymerization favors groups that stabilize a carbocation, so the phenyl-substituted styrene is most reactive and the ester-substituted monomer least.

choices.text: H2C=CHCl < H2C=CHCO2CH3 < H2C=CH–C6H5 < H2C=CHCH3
choices.why: The ester group is the most electron-withdrawing here, so H2C=CHCO2CH3 is least reactive, and styrene, whose phenyl ring best stabilizes the carbocation, is most reactive.

choices.text: H2C=CHCO2CH3 < H2C=CHCH3 < H2C=CHCl < H2C=CH–C6H5
choices.why: Propene's methyl group stabilizes a carbocation better than chlorine does, so H2C=CHCH3 is more reactive than H2C=CHCl.

explanation: Cationic polymerization needs groups that stabilize the chain-carrying carbocation. The answer to Exercise 31.1.1 gives the order H2C=CHCO2CH3 < H2C=CHCl < H2C=CHCH3 < H2C=CH–C6H5: the electron-withdrawing ester makes methyl acrylate least reactive, and styrene is most reactive.

prompt: Which order correctly ranks these monomers from least to most reactive toward anionic polymerization: H2C=CHCH3, H2C=CHC≡N, H2C=CHC6H5?

choices.text: H2C=CHCH3 < H2C=CHC6H5 < H2C=CHC≡N
H2C=CHC≡N < H2C=CHC6H5 < H2C=CHCH3
choices.why: This is the reverse order. Anionic polymerization favors electron-withdrawing groups, so acrylonitrile is the most reactive and propene the least.

choices.text: H2C=CHC6H5 < H2C=CHCH3 < H2C=CHC≡N
choices.why: Styrene can be polymerized anionically (its benzylic anion is resonance-stabilized), so it is more reactive than propene, whose methyl group gives no such help.

choices.text: H2C=CHCH3 < H2C=CHC≡N < H2C=CHC6H5
choices.why: The cyano group is a strong electron-withdrawing group, so acrylonitrile is the most reactive of the three toward anionic polymerization.

explanation: Anionic polymerization works with vinyl monomers that have electron-withdrawing groups. The answer to Exercise 31.1.2 gives H2C=CHCH3 < H2C=CHC6H5 < H2C=CHC≡N: propene has no group to stabilize an anion, and acrylonitrile's –C≡N group is strongly electron-withdrawing.

prompt: In the anionic polymerization of styrene with butyllithium, how is the chain-carrying intermediate stabilized?

choices.text: It is a benzylic carbanion, stabilized by resonance with the aromatic ring
It is a benzylic carbocation, stabilized by resonance with the aromatic ring
choices.why: Butyllithium is an anionic initiator, so the intermediate carries a negative charge, not a positive one.

choices.text: It is a radical stabilized by the lithium atom
choices.why: Butyllithium starts an anionic, not a radical, polymerization. The negative charge is spread into the ring by resonance.

choices.text: The negative charge sits on a terminal CH2 carbon far from the ring
choices.why: When the anion adds to the CH2 end of styrene, the charge ends up on the carbon bearing the phenyl group, where resonance can spread it into the ring.

explanation: The answer to Exercise 31.1.3 shows that the intermediate is a resonance-stabilized benzylic carbanion: the negative charge is on the carbon attached to the phenyl ring and is delocalized into the ring by resonance.
